title: About
text:
I am a bioinformatician and computational biologist with a background spanning genomics, epigenetics, scientific software and research computing.
I started in biology and moved into bioinformatics at a time when the field itself was rapidly changing. Over the years, my work has changed from individual data analyses to developing pipelines and software, managing data, working on large collaborative projects, and eventually building and leading a bioinformatics core facility.
I have always been interested in the space between the biological question and the computational solution: understanding the science, working with the data, choosing or developing the right tools, and creating the systems that allow this work to be done reproducibly and sustainably.


My scientific background is in genomics and molecular biology, with a strong focus on epigenomics and gene regulation. I have worked with genomic and epigenomic data across hematopoiesis, leukemia and cancer, as well as other biomedical research areas.
Much of my work has involved DNA methylation, alongside transcriptomics and other functional genomics approaches.



As bioinformatics has evolved, so has my work.
What started with data analysis and computational methods increasingly expanded into scientific software, reproducible workflows, data management, HPC environments and research infrastructure.
Leading a bioinformatics core facility made these connections very visible. Good bioinformatics depends not only on the analysis itself, but also on how data enters a project, how workflows are run, how results are documented, how software and data are maintained, and how scientists and technical teams work together.
This broader view of computational research is now an essential part of how I think about bioinformatics.



I am currently extending my background towards machine learning and AI-enabled biomedical research.
My interest is not in AI as a separate discipline, but in how these methods can become useful parts of scientific practice — integrated with biological knowledge, research data, computational workflows and reproducible infrastructure.



I write about some of these ideas in Building Bioinformatics, where I reflect on bioinformatics, software engineering, workflows and research infrastructure.
I am also documenting what I am learning about machine learning and generative AI in Catching up with AI.
For a more structured overview of my work, see Projects, Experience, or my CV.

title: Experience
text:
My work experience spans quite different research environments: from basic and discovery research, through high-throughput genomics at a sequencing centre, to building and leading a bioinformatics core facility within a translational biomedical research institute.




2021–2025



Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute (IJC), Barcelona
I built and led the institute’s bioinformatics core facility, supporting research groups across leukemia, immunology and other biomedical research areas.
My role combined scientific bioinformatics with team leadership and research support, as well as developing the processes, workflows and infrastructure needed to provide a sustainable bioinformatics service.
The work ranged from individual research projects to developing some of the broader bioinformatics environment within the institute, including data management, reproducible workflows, computational infrastructure, training and collaboration with experimental scientists and clinicians.







2013–2019



National Centre for Genomic Analysis (CNAG-CRG), Barcelona
I worked in a sequencing-centre environment on large-scale genomics and epigenomics projects, with a particular focus on DNA methylation and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing.
Much of my work was connected to the BLUEPRINT Epigenome project and the study of DNA methylation during hematopoietic differentiation and in leukemia. I also worked on projects in other biomedical research areas such as Inflammatory Bowels Disease (IBD).
Working at a sequencing centre brought together biological research with the computational challenges of processing large volumes of sequencing data. My work included data analysis, computational methods and the development of pipelines and software, including contributions to gemBS and gemBSR.







2012–2013



RIKEN Omics Science Center, Yokohama
I worked on the computational analysis of transcription and transposable element activity during early zebrafish development, integrating CAGE and ChIP-seq data.




2009–2012



Centre for Genomic Regulation (CRG), Barcelona
I worked on transcriptomics and alternative splicing as part of the ENCODE project, developing and applying computational methods for large-scale RNA-seq analysis.
This included work on GRAPE, a computational pipeline developed for the analysis of RNA-seq data within ENCODE.







PhD · 2008



University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand
My doctoral research focused on microsatellite evolution, combining molecular biology with computational approaches to study short tandem repeats in yeast.
It was during my PhD that I increasingly moved towards computational biology and bioinformatics.
